summary: The stages of the system development life cycle and how the waterfall, agile and spiral models organise them.

theory.title: What the system development life cycle is

blocks.content: A structured sequence of **stages** that a team follows to **plan, build, introduce and maintain** a new information system. Each stage has clear activities and produces documents or products that the next stage uses.

items.title: Why follow an SDLC?
items.content:
- Breaks a large project into **manageable stages** with clear goals.
- Makes sure the system **meets the users' requirements**.
- Lets managers **plan time, cost and staff** and check progress at **milestones**.
- Produces **documentation** at every stage, so the system can be maintained later.
- Finds problems **early**, when they are cheaper to fix.

items.title: Who is involved?
items.content:
- **Client / end users** — describe their needs, test and use the system.
- **Systems analyst** — studies the current system and writes the requirements.
- **Designer** — plans the interface, data and processes.
- **Programmers / developers** — write the code and build the database.
- **Testers** — check that the system works and meets the requirements.
- **Project manager** — plans, schedules and controls the project.

blocks.content:
flowchart LR
  A[1 Analysis] --> B[2 Design] --> C[3 Development and testing] --> D[4 Implementation] --> E[5 Documentation] --> F[6 Evaluation and maintenance]
  F -. new requirements .-> A
blocks.caption: The six stages form a cycle — evaluation can start the next version

blocks.title: Same stages, different organisation
blocks.content: Every development model uses the **same stages**. What differs is **how they are organised**: done once in a strict order (**waterfall**), repeated in short cycles (**agile**), or repeated in loops driven by risk (**spiral**).
The analyst finds out **what the current system does, what is wrong with it and what the new system must do**.

blocks.title: Activities in the analysis stage
items: **Investigate the current system** using questionnaires, interviews, observation and examining documents.
Identify the **problems** of the current system and the **needs** of the users.
Identify **inputs, processes, outputs and storage** (often shown in a data flow diagram).
Carry out a **feasibility study** — is the project worth doing?
Produce the **requirements specification**, agreed with the client.

blocks.title: Feasibility study (TELOS)
rows: Do the hardware, software and skills exist to build it?
Do the benefits outweigh the costs? Is it within the budget?
Does it follow the law (e.g. personal data protection)?
Will the users actually be able and willing to use it?
Can it be finished by the deadline?

blocks.title: A requirements specification (extract) — online library
blocks.content:
1. The system must allow students to **search** books by title, author or ISBN.
2. The system must let librarians **record loans and returns** by scanning barcodes.
3. The system must **email a reminder** two days before a book is due.
4. A search must return results in **under 2 seconds**.
5. Only staff accounts may **edit** book records.
Requirements must be **specific and testable** — they are used again at the evaluation stage to decide whether the project succeeded.

theory.title: Stages 2 and 3 — Design, development and testing

blocks.content: The designer decides **how** the system will meet the requirements — before any code is written.

blocks.title: What is designed
rows: ERD, normalised tables, **data dictionary** (field names, types, sizes, validation rules)
Screen layouts, input forms, report layouts, **prototypes**
Validation rules, access levels, passwords, backups
**Test plan** with normal, boundary and erroneous data and expected results

blocks.content: Programmers **build** the system from the design: write the code, create the database, connect the interface. Testers then check it.

blocks.title: Kinds of testing
rows: Each module / function on its own
The whole system against the requirements
By the developers' own team, in-house, before release
By a limited group of **real users** in real conditions, before full release
By the **client**, to confirm the system meets the requirements before it is accepted

blocks.title: Test data
blocks.content: Each test uses **normal** (valid, typical), **boundary/extreme** (at the limits) and **erroneous** (invalid) data, recorded in the test plan with the **expected** and the **actual** result.

theory.title: Stages 4–6 — Implementation, documentation, evaluation and maintenance

blocks.content: The new system is **installed and put into use**: hardware and software are installed, existing data is **converted and transferred**, and users are **trained**. A changeover method is chosen:

blocks.title: Changeover methods
rows: Old system stopped, new one started at once
Both run together for a time; results compared
New system used in one part of the organisation first
New system introduced one module at a time

blocks.title: Two kinds of documentation
rows: The people who use the system
Program code with comments, algorithms, data dictionary, ERD/DFDs, hardware and software requirements, test results
How to install and log in, how to carry out each task, screenshots, error messages and what to do, FAQ, backup procedures, troubleshooting

blocks.content: The finished system is compared with the **requirements specification**: Does it do everything it should? Is it fast, reliable and easy to use? User feedback is collected; strengths, weaknesses and improvements are recorded.

items.title: Corrective
items.content: Fixing **bugs** found after the system is in use.

items.title: Adaptive
items.content: Changing the system to fit a **new environment** — a new OS, new law, new tax rate, new hardware.

items.title: Perfective
items.content: **Improving** the system — new features, better performance or interface, at the users' request.

blocks.content: "Name the stage" questions use key words: *feasibility, requirements* → **analysis**; *ERD, data dictionary, test plan, screen layout* → **design**; *coding, testing* → **development**; *training, data transfer, changeover* → **implementation**; *user guide* → **documentation**; *compare with requirements, bug fixes* → **evaluation and maintenance**.

A **linear, sequential** model: the stages are carried out **one after another, in a fixed order**. Each stage must be **completed and signed off** before the next starts, and the project does not normally go back to an earlier stage.

flowchart TB
  R[Requirements and analysis] --> D[Design] --> I[Implementation — coding] --> V[Testing] --> P[Deployment] --> M[Maintenance]
blocks.caption: Waterfall — each stage flows down into the next

items: Each stage produces **complete documentation** (requirements, design documents) before the next stage begins.
**Milestones** at the end of each stage make progress easy to measure.
The client is involved mainly **at the beginning** (requirements) and **at the end** (acceptance).
**Testing happens late**, after all the code is written.

blocks.title: Waterfall
rows: **Inflexible** — changing requirements later is difficult and expensive
Clear **structure**: a stage is completed before the next one starts
The client sees a **working product only at the end**
Each stage has **clear deliverables and milestones**
Errors in requirements or design are found **late**, during testing
**Cost and time** are easier to estimate
Long projects risk delivering a system that no longer fits the users' needs
Thorough **documentation** helps maintenance and new staff
Not suitable for complex projects where requirements are uncertain

blocks.title: When waterfall fits
blocks.content: A ministry orders a system to calculate a new tax: the rules are **fixed by law**, the requirements are clear from the start, and **detailed documentation** is required. Waterfall is suitable.

An **iterative and incremental** approach: the system is built in **short cycles (iterations or sprints)**, usually 1–4 weeks. Each cycle delivers a **working part** of the system, which the client reviews; the plan is adjusted after every cycle.

flowchart TB
  B[(Product backlog)] --> P[Sprint planning]
  P --> W[Design, build, test]
  W --> R[Sprint review with the client]
  R --> RE[Retrospective]
  RE --> P
  R --> S[Working increment of the software]
blocks.caption: Each sprint repeats plan, design, build, test and review

items.title: Roles
items.content: **Product owner** — represents the client, decides priorities. **Scrum master** — removes obstacles, keeps the process. **Development team** — designs, builds and tests.

items.title: Artefacts
items.content: **Product backlog** — prioritised list of all wanted features (user stories). **Sprint backlog** — the features chosen for this sprint. **Increment** — working software at the end of the sprint.

items.title: Events
items.content: **Sprint planning**, a short **daily stand-up** meeting (what I did, what I will do, problems), **sprint review** with the client, **retrospective** (how to work better).

blocks.title: A user story
blocks.content: "As a **student**, I want to **see my homework for the week** so that **I can plan my time**." The team estimates it, builds it in one sprint and shows it to the teacher at the review.

blocks.title: Agile
rows: Final **cost and deadline are hard to predict**
The client is **involved throughout** and gives regular feedback
Needs the client to be **available often**
**Working software early** — the most important features first
**Less documentation**, which can make maintenance harder
Needs an experienced, self-organised team; hard for very large teams

blocks.content: A **risk-driven, iterative** model (Barry Boehm, 1986). The project goes round a **spiral of loops**; every loop passes through **four phases**, and each loop produces a **more complete prototype** until the final system is built.

blocks.title: The four phases of each loop
items: **Determine objectives** — requirements and alternatives for this loop.
**Identify and resolve risks** — analyse what could go wrong (technical, cost, schedule); build a **prototype** or run a study to reduce the risk.
**Develop and test** — design, code and test the next version.
**Plan the next iteration** — the client **evaluates** the result; decide whether and how to continue.

blocks.content:
flowchart TB
  O[1 Objectives] --> R[2 Risk analysis + prototype]
  R --> D[3 Develop and test]
  D --> P[4 Evaluate and plan]
  P -- next loop --> O
  P -- complete --> F([Final system])
blocks.caption: Every loop passes through the four phases; each new loop builds a more complete version

blocks.title: Example — three loops for an online banking app
rows: Will customers understand and accept the idea?
Paper/screen **prototype** of the main screens, approved by the client
Is the payment process secure and fast enough?
Working prototype of log-in and payments, security tested
Can the system handle thousands of users at once?

blocks.title: Spiral
rows: **Risk analysis in every loop** — high-risk problems found early
Suitable for **large, complex and high-risk** projects
The number of loops — and so the end date — is uncertain
Requirements can be refined in each loop
Changes can be added in later loops
Success depends heavily on good risk analysis

blocks.title: Waterfall vs agile vs spiral
rows: At the end of each loop
Small/medium projects with clear, stable requirements
Projects with changing requirements and an available client

blocks.title: Choosing a model for a scenario
rows: A school library system; the requirements are fully known and will not change
Clear requirements; simple to manage and document
A start-up's mobile app; features change after users try each version
Frequent change and feedback; early releases
A new air-traffic control or banking payment system
Very high risk and cost; risk analysis in every loop
A government system whose rules are set by law and need full documentation
A school app for teachers who want to see each feature and suggest changes

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Name two benefits of using a waterfall model. [2]**
1. It has a **clear structure** — each stage is **completed before** the next begins.
2. It is **easy to manage**, with **clear milestones** and documentation for every stage.

**Q: Explain one disadvantage of the agile model for a client. [2]**
The client must **take part in reviews regularly** throughout the project (1), **which takes up a lot of their time** / and the final cost is hard to predict because requirements keep changing (1).

**Q: Explain why the spiral model is suitable for developing software for a bank. [2]**
The project is **high-risk and expensive** (1), and the spiral model **analyses and reduces risks in every loop** using prototypes before the full system is built (1).

- Saying agile has **no** planning or documentation — it has **less**, and plans each sprint.
- Confusing **prototyping** with agile: prototypes are used in several models (especially spiral).
- Giving an advantage without linking it to the **scenario** when the question describes one.

blocks.title: Check yourself
items: List the six SDLC stages in order and one output of each.
What does each letter of TELOS stand for?
What is the difference between alpha, beta and acceptance testing?
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of each model.
Which model would you choose for a project with very high risk? Why?

questions.title: Order of SDLC stages
questions.text: Which sequence shows the stages of the system development life cycle in the correct order?

content.hint: You must understand the problem before you can plan a solution.

scheme.explanation: The problem is investigated (analysis) before the solution is planned (design), built (development), checked (testing) and installed (implementation).

questions.title: Output of the analysis stage
questions.text: State the main document produced at the end of the **analysis** stage.

content.hint: It lists what the new system must do.

scheme.mark_scheme: Requirements specification (accept: system requirements / requirements document / user requirements).
scheme.explanation: Analysis investigates the problem and records what the new system must do in a requirements specification, which is the input to the design stage.

questions.title: Match stages to activities
questions.text: Match each SDLC stage to the activity that takes place in it.

right.text: Interviewing users and observing the current system
Producing input screen layouts and data structures
Running the program with normal, boundary and erroneous data
Changing the system after it is in use to fix newly found errors

scheme.mark_scheme: Analysis–R1, Design–R2, Testing–R3, Maintenance–R4. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Agile and requirements
questions.text: In the agile model, all requirements must be fixed and signed off before any code is written.

scheme.explanation: Fixed, signed-off requirements are a feature of the waterfall model. Agile expects requirements to change and adapts the plan after each iteration.

questions.title: Distinctive feature of the spiral model
questions.text: Which feature most clearly distinguishes the spiral model from the other development models?

options.content: It produces working software at the end of each sprint
It completes each stage fully before moving on
It includes a risk-analysis phase in every iteration
It does not require any documentation

scheme.explanation: Risk analysis in each loop is the defining characteristic of the spiral model.

questions.title: Disadvantages of waterfall
questions.text: Select **two** disadvantages of the waterfall model.

options.content: The client does not see a working system until late in the project
Changes to requirements during development are difficult and costly

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Explain an advantage of agile
questions.text: Explain **one** advantage of using the agile model rather than the waterfall model.

scheme.mark_scheme:
1 mark for identifying an advantage; 1 mark for explaining why it is an advantage / how it arises.

Examples:
- Can respond to changing requirements (1) because the plan is reviewed after each short iteration (1).
- Client sees working parts early (1) so misunderstandings are found and corrected before much time/money is wasted (1).
- Working parts can be used before the project ends (1) because each iteration delivers a usable increment (1).

points.criterion: Identifies a valid advantage of agile over waterfall
Explains why/how this advantage arises (expansion linked to iterations or client feedback)

scheme.model_answer: Agile can cope with changing requirements, because the system is built in short iterations and the client reviews each one, so new or changed requirements can be included in the next iteration instead of having to restart the project.
scheme.ai_instructions: Award the second mark only if the expansion explains the mechanism (short iterations, regular client feedback, incremental delivery). A second advantage without expansion does not earn the second mark.

questions.title: Choose a model for a hospital system
questions.text:
A hospital is commissioning a large system that controls the dosage of medicines given to patients. The system is expensive to build and errors could endanger lives. Some requirements are not yet fully understood.

Discuss which development model (waterfall, agile or spiral) is most suitable for this project. Justify your answer.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Up to 4 marks. Expected choice: **spiral** (accept a well-justified alternative, maximum 3 marks).

- Identifies spiral as most suitable (1)
- Justification linked to risk: risk analysis in every loop reduces the danger of errors in a safety-critical system (1)
- Justification linked to size/cost: suitable for large, expensive projects (1)
- Justification linked to unclear requirements: prototypes/iterations allow requirements to be refined (1)
- Comparison point: why waterfall (fixed requirements) or agile (less up-front risk analysis/documentation) is less suitable (1)

points.criterion: Chooses the spiral model (or a justified alternative)
Links risk analysis to the safety-critical nature of the system
Links model to the large/expensive scale of the project
Links iterations/prototypes to the requirements that are not fully understood
Explains why another model is less suitable

scheme.model_answer: The spiral model is most suitable. Because errors could endanger patients, the risk-analysis phase in every loop means hazards are identified and reduced before each new part is built. The project is large and expensive, which is the kind of project spiral is designed for. As some requirements are unclear, each loop can produce a prototype that doctors evaluate, refining the requirements. Waterfall would be unsuitable because it needs all requirements fixed at the start, and agile performs less formal risk analysis and documentation, which a safety-critical system needs.
scheme.ai_instructions: Maximum 4 marks. Points must be applied to the hospital scenario; generic statements about a model that are not linked to the scenario earn at most 1 mark in total. If the student chooses agile or waterfall, award a maximum of 3 marks for justification that is accurate and linked to the scenario.
scheme.explanation: A 'discuss' question needs a decision and justification applied to the context, ideally with a counter-point about the alternatives.
